channel.title: Signal Brief · AI
channel.description: Signal Brief: the day in technology, in The Signal's own words. Every item is written from linked official sources and fact checked before publication.

item.title: ChatGPT Wallet lets agents pay without seeing your card details
item.description: OpenAI has introduced ChatGPT Wallet, a way for its Dots agents to pay for purchases on a user's behalf without seeing the user's actual card details. Users add a card once and approve each purchase with a security check such as Face ID or a fingerprint, after which the payment network issues a token in place of the real card number. The wallet starts with ChatGPT Pro subscribers in the US, built with American Express, Mastercard and Visa, and OpenAI has published a Commerce Partner Playbook to help businesses accept agent payments. Why it matters for tech: Agent-led shopping only works if payments are safe and merchants can accept them, so a wallet built on existing card rails is the missing piece for agentic commerce.

item.title: Anthropic opens a private beta for self-hosted Claude Managed Agents
item.description: Anthropic has opened a private beta of self-hosted Claude Managed Agents, letting companies run the whole agent service inside their own cloud or data centre. The harness, sandboxes, credentials and session history all run on the customer's infrastructure, while model calls still go to a provider the customer chooses, such as Anthropic, Amazon Bedrock, Google's Agent Platform or Microsoft Foundry. Access is limited to eligible organisations through their Anthropic account team, and the server licence requires customers to roll back a version within eight hours of a safety notice. Why it matters for tech: Teams that want long-running agents working on internal code can now keep the control plane behind their own security perimeter instead of handing it to a vendor.

item.title: llama.cpp reaches 1.0 with a stability promise for local AI builders
item.description: The llama.cpp project has released version 1.0.0 of its libraries, committing to semantic versioning so that breaking changes to the public C API will only arrive with major version bumps. The project, which lets developers run multimodal language models on hardware from consumer laptops to enterprise servers, now supports more than 150 model architecture variants. The release also covers ggml 1.0.0, the tensor library underneath it. Why it matters for tech: Local and private AI products depend on llama.cpp, so a stable API gives their builders a firmer foundation to build on.

item.title: Google launches Gemini 4 Hydrogen, a faster model built for agentic coding work
item.description: Google DeepMind has introduced Gemini 4 Hydrogen, a model aimed at everyday coding and multi-step agent workflows rather than long-horizon reasoning, which stays with the Carbon and Argon models. Hydrogen runs across the Gemini API, AI Studio, the Gemini app and Google Search, with a 1 million token context window priced at $1.50 per million input tokens and $7.50 per million output tokens. On Terminal-Bench 4.1 it scored 57%, against 18.2% for Gemini 3.8 Flash, and Google says it completes tasks about 2.5 times faster at its default setting. Why it matters for tech: A cheaper, quicker execution model changes the economics of running agents all day, since most agent work is routine execution rather than deep reasoning.

item.title: Google opens preorders for Gemini smartglasses starting at $395
item.description: Google has opened preorders for its first Gemini-powered smartglasses, built with Samsung, Gentle Monster and Warby Parker, with shipping and store availability from December 10. The glasses have no in-lens display; wearers talk to Gemini by voice, use touch controls, or use a 12 megapixel camera. Warby Parker frames start at $395 in the US and Gentle Monster styles at $449, and Google says the camera has an always-on recording light, a physical off switch, no livestreaming and no real-time face recognition. Why it matters for tech: Glasses put an AI assistant on the face rather than in the hand, so the privacy controls Google ships with them set the pattern other makers will be judged against.

item.title: Google DeepMind launches AlphaGenome 2 to predict DNA effects in single cell types
item.description: Google DeepMind has announced AlphaGenome 2, a DNA sequence model that predicts how genetic variants affect specific human cell types rather than broad tissue averages. Trained on more than 100 million individual cell profiles across 68 tissues, it identified nearly twice as many causal variants on a single-cell immune dataset, 30% against 16% for the original model. The model is available now for non-commercial research through the AlphaGenome API, and in private preview for commercial research. Why it matters for tech: Cell-level variant prediction helps researchers connect disease-linked DNA changes to the exact cells where they act, which broad tissue models miss.

item.title: Google launches Gemini Decisions API for fast yes or no and scoring calls
item.description: Google has introduced the Gemini Decisions API, powered by its new Gemini Decision 1 model, which scores up to 1,000 yes or no, multiple choice and rubric questions against one multimodal input in a single pass. It returns probabilities and confidence scores with 150 to 250 milliseconds of end-to-end latency, priced at $0.10 per million input tokens with no output tokens billed. The API is available through the Gemini API in Google AI Studio, and Google already uses it for model routing, design iteration and safety checks on tools. Why it matters for tech: Scoring options instead of generating text makes routine agent decisions such as routing, policy checks and grading faster and cheaper, and the confidence scores let code send uncertain cases to a human.

item.title: Google rolls out Gemini 4 Carbon with an agent swarm for coding
item.description: Google has made Gemini 4 Carbon publicly available to Gemini app users and to developers through the Gemini API, AI Studio and Vertex AI, after an earlier limited release for cybersecurity work. The model is aimed at agentic coding, including building apps and prototypes and debugging code. Google cites 87.9% on SWE-Bench Verified, against 81% for the previous Gemini 4 Argon, and says one master agent can coordinate up to 10,000 agents that plan, work in parallel and check each other's work. Pricing is $2 per million input tokens and $12 per million output tokens. Why it matters for tech: A coding model that coordinates large agent teams changes how much of a build can be handed to agents at once, and the published benchmark figures give teams a concrete basis for comparing it with the previous release.

item.title: ChatGPT gains verified Business Agents with in-chat checkout
item.description: OpenAI has launched Businesses in ChatGPT in beta, adding verified AI Business Agents that represent companies inside ChatGPT and carry a verified blue checkmark. Users can browse a business directory, ask questions, compare products and complete purchases with instant checkout without leaving the chat. Launch partners named by OpenAI include Etsy, Target, Walmart, Shopify, Zillow, Expedia, Booking.com, Canva and Figma. The feature is available from November 10 to ChatGPT users in the US, free and paid, at no additional charge. Why it matters for tech: Putting storefronts and checkout inside a chatbot turns ChatGPT into a shopping channel, which matters for retailers deciding whether to build an agent and for rivals watching how conversational commerce takes shape.

item.title: Anthropic launches Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 for coding, finance and science
item.description: Anthropic has released Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2, which it describes as its most capable models for coding, finance and science. Fable 5.2 is available now, while Mythos 5.2 is limited to vetted organizations. In pre-release testing cited by Anthropic, Fable 5.2 migrated three complex devices in a day where Claude Sonnet 4.5 managed one, and completed a 30-hour proof of Fermat's Last Theorem. Why it matters for tech: A new top-tier coding model with a published test record gives developers a concrete alternative to compare against current coding models on speed and long-task stamina.

item.title: Meta launches Muse Ember, a small model for agentic coding
item.description: Meta has launched Muse Ember (muse-ember-1.0), a small model built for agentic coding, available through Meta's Models API and Amazon Bedrock, with Azure and Google Cloud to follow. It carries a 1 million token context window and up to 512,000 output tokens, priced at $0.10 per million input tokens and $0.50 per million output tokens. On Meta's Intelligence Index benchmark it scored 36 at $0.14 per task, the same score as Claude Haiku at $0.41 per task. Why it matters for tech: A cheaper model that matches a larger rival on Meta's own benchmark puts price pressure on coding agents and widens the choice of small models for everyday coding work.

item.title: Apple pushes Siri toward agentic tasks, report says
item.description: Bloomberg reports that Apple chief executive John Ternus is pressing AI chief Craig Federighi to speed up the Siri roadmap and deliver an assistant that can act on its own, rivalling OpenAI's Dots and Meta's Muse. Fine-grained control of Apple's own apps, such as editing photos and organising Safari tabs, is reported to arrive with iOS 27.3, while control of third-party apps, such as placing a food order or booking a table, is reported to follow in the spring. Bloomberg's Mark Gurman writes that Siri could become more like an agent as early as next year. Why it matters for tech: Siri is the assistant built into Apple's devices, so turning it into an assistant that carries out multi-step tasks changes what phone assistants are expected to do.

item.title: DeepMind AI agents find two weaknesses in retired 1024-bit RSA
item.description: Google DeepMind says AI agents working under human supervision found two weaknesses in legacy 1024-bit RSA encryption, a key size the industry retired years ago. In a sandbox test, the agents reproduced a signature forgery on a solved benchmark key using 3.5 times less CPU time, and a new algorithm improved on the previous best method by roughly 1,600 times in theoretical estimates for short fingerprints, while a second result cuts the average cost of factoring each additional 1024-bit key by about 30 times. DeepMind states modern 2048-bit and larger keys are unaffected and no live systems were touched. Why it matters for tech: AI agents are now doing original cryptanalysis in weeks, so hardness assumptions need continuous re-testing rather than being treated as fixed.

item.title: Thinking Machines Lab ships Inkling 2 Small, with open weights promised next week
item.description: Thinking Machines Lab has released Inkling 2 Small, a mixture-of-experts model with 594 billion total parameters and 17 billion active per token, which takes text and image input. The lab reports a score of 31 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index and says the model is built for long autonomous coding and research tasks. It is available now through the lab's Tinker platform with closed weights, and the lab says it intends to release the full weights under an Apache 2.0 licence next week, after external safety testing and red-teaming. Why it matters for tech: The model is built for hours-long autonomous coding work, and its weights stay closed until safety testing finishes, so the open release is conditional rather than immediate.

item.title: Perplexity launches always on work agents called Teammates
item.description: Perplexity has launched Teammates, always on AI agents built for work that can take on different roles in a workspace at the same time. Each Teammate works from its own thread in the Perplexity app and can draw on existing projects, skills and memory, and users can talk to them in Slack. Access is limited to the $200 a month Max plan, and chief executive Aravind Srinivas said on X that he sees organisations eventually having hundreds of Teammates working for each person. Why it matters for tech: Work agents are moving from single chatbots to teams of agents with their own roles, and Perplexity is charging a premium for the shift.

item.title: Meta Muse can now build custom spaces from a description
item.description: Meta has added spaces to its Muse assistant, letting users describe an app such as a shopping hub, a school dashboard or a trivia game and have Muse build it. Connected apps such as Gmail, Google Calendar, OpenTable and Notion let Muse keep the details in a space current in the background, and users can tick items off, add notes and place spaces in the sidebar or on a schedule. Meta also said Active Memory and Active Focus, capabilities from its Muse Wonder model, are coming to the Muse app and the Meta AI chatbot. Why it matters for tech: Assistants are turning into personalised workspaces that stay current on their own, which raises the bar for what a chatbot is expected to do.

item.title: Cognition ships a cheaper coding model but keeps its weights private
item.description: Cognition has released SWE-2 Flash, a coding model it says costs a fifth as much as its larger SWE-2 model and generates tokens about three times faster. Flash is built on Thinking Machines Lab’s open weight Inkling Small model, yet Cognition is keeping its own weights private, citing cybersecurity concerns. On Cognition’s own figures, Flash scored 20% on Terminal Bench 4.0 against 0.9% for the base model, and 89.9% on SWE Bench Pro v2 Hard, close to SWE-2’s 90.6%. Why it matters for tech: A model built on an open base with closed weights tests how far openness extends in practice, and whether cheaper coding models can match their larger siblings.

item.title: OpenAI launches GPT-6 Cyber, a security model built to stay inside its authorised scope
item.description: OpenAI introduced GPT-6 Cyber, a model for finding exploitable vulnerabilities and developing fixes, trained to stay within the scope researchers set. It scores 48.5% on ExploitGym, up from 32.1% for GPT-5.6 Cyber, and avoided out of scope services in 99.93% of alignment tests without deployment prompts. It already helped find 81 previously unknown high severity Firefox flaws, and it is initially available through the API and Codex to approved Daybreak Red customers. Why it matters for tech: Security models that can find flaws are only useful if they can be trusted not to wander, and this one pairs stronger exploit skills with measured restraint.

item.description: Google made Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash generally available across the Gemini API and Google Cloud. It creates and edits video clips up to 15 seconds long, up from 10 seconds, with multi turn conversational editing and stronger reference consistency. The price falls 30% from version 1.1, to $0.07 per second for 720p video. Why it matters for tech: Video generation is moving from short demos toward usable ad and product clips, with editing and pricing aimed at production use.

item.title: Claude can now read your bank account, with read only access through Plaid
item.description: Anthropic launched Personal Finance in Claude in beta, connecting the chatbot to bank and card accounts through Plaid. Claude can break down spending by category, say which bills remain before payday, and judge whether a large purchase is affordable, using up to two years of transaction history. Access is read only: Claude cannot move, manage or invest money, and it does not see banking passwords. The beta is rolling out this week to Claude Pro, Max and Ultra subscribers in the US. Why it matters for tech: AI assistants are moving from answering questions to acting on personal financial data, which makes read only access and clear limits the story.

item.title: New benchmark finds frontier models lose track of changing facts in long documents
item.description: Allen AI's StateBench tests how well language models track information that changes across long documents, across four levels of difficulty. Frontier models including Gemini 3.8 Flash, Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 handled simple updates but fell to 13 percent accuracy or lower on the hardest problems at the longest lengths, while recurrent and hybrid architectures generalised further when trained on the task. Why it matters for tech: Long document and agent work depends on exactly this state tracking, so the failure mode matters well beyond the benchmark.
item.content:encoded:
Allen AI's StateBench tests how well language models track information that changes across long documents, across four levels of difficulty. Frontier models including Gemini 3.8 Flash, Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 handled simple updates but fell to 13 percent accuracy or lower on the hardest problems at the longest lengths, while recurrent and hybrid architectures generalised further when trained on the task.

Why it matters for tech: Long document and agent work depends on exactly this state tracking, so the failure mode matters well beyond the benchmark.

Source:

  • Hugging Face Blog (Allen AI)

item.title: OpenAI raises bug bounty rewards for security researchers
item.description: OpenAI is increasing payouts under its Security Bug Bounty programme and adding bonuses tied to report quality, researcher loyalty and priority campaigns. The programme pays independent researchers who find and report vulnerabilities in OpenAI products and services. Why it matters for tech: Bigger rewards pull more skilled researchers toward finding flaws in widely used AI systems before attackers do.

item.title: Anthropic adds Claude Code limits aimed at game cloning
item.description: Anthropic has confirmed new restrictions in Claude Code that stop the tool from reproducing existing video games, after its Opus 5.5 model began blocking game recreation requests. Some users report that generic reverse engineering tasks are also being blocked, and an Anthropic employee said the company is iterating to find the right balance. Why it matters for tech: It is a live example of a model maker enforcing copyright limits inside a coding tool, with false positives already hitting legitimate work.
